To suppurate means to form and discharge pus. When a wound, a sore, or an infected part of the body suppurates, it is actively producing and oozing that thick, yellowish or greenish fluid you see coming out of badly infected cuts, boils, or abscesses.

In the simplest terms: if something is suppurating, it is festering with infection and leaking pus.

To really get this word, you need to understand what pus is, because suppuration is entirely about pus.

When bacteria invade your tissue — say, through a cut — your immune system sends a flood of white blood cells (mainly neutrophils) to destroy them. These cells attack and kill the bacteria, but in doing so, they also die themselves. The result is a thick, creamy buildup of dead white blood cells, dead bacteria, dead tissue, and fluid. That buildup is pus. It is, in a very literal sense, the battlefield aftermath of your immune system's war against infection.

The infected area swells up, becomes red and warm, and eventually the pressure builds until the pus either bursts through the skin on its own or is drained by a doctor. The entire process — the forming of pus and its release — is what "to suppurate" describes.

Suppuration can occur anywhere in or on the body where there is a bacterial infection that the immune system is fighting with this kind of inflammatory response. Common examples include:

Skin and surface wounds: A cut that was not cleaned properly can become infected and begin to suppurate after a few days. You will notice swelling, redness, heat, and eventually pus oozing from the site.

Boils (furuncles): A boil is a classic example of suppuration. It starts as a hard, red, painful lump under the skin and gradually suppurates — forming a visible, soft "head" filled with pus — before bursting.

Abscesses: An abscess is basically a pocket of pus trapped inside body tissue. Whether it forms in the gum (a dental abscess), the skin, or internally near an organ, it suppurates by collecting and releasing that pus. Doctors often lance (cut open) abscesses to allow proper drainage.

Infected internal sites: Suppuration is not only a surface event. Deep tissues, bones (in a condition called osteomyelitis), the middle ear (in serious ear infections), and even organs can suppurate — making it a serious medical concern when it occurs internally.
How It Is Used in Sentences

The word is mostly found in medical or literary writing, and occasionally in formal journalism. Here are examples that show how it works in practice:

  • "The doctor examined the wound and confirmed it had begun to suppurate, requiring immediate antibiotics and cleaning."
  • "Left untreated, the deep scratch suppurated over the course of several days."
  • "The abscess was suppurating so severely that surgery was the only option."
  • "His infected tooth began to suppurate, and the pain became unbearable."

Notice that it can be used in the past tense (suppurated), the present continuous (is suppurating), or as a descriptor of a condition that is actively happening.

Writers — especially literary and journalistic ones — sometimes use "suppurate" metaphorically to describe something non-physical that has been allowed to fester, grow worse, and eventually erupt in a damaging way. The image being invoked is the same: something rotten building up pressure until it releases.

For example:

  • "The unresolved tension between the two departments had been suppurating for years before it finally exploded into a public dispute."
  • "Injustice, left unaddressed, suppurates — it doesn't simply disappear."

In these cases, the writer is comparing a worsening social, emotional, or political situation to a wound that is slowly filling with pus. The word carries a sense of something being allowed to rot from within.

Since you want to understand this word completely, you should also know its close relatives:

Suppuration (noun) — the process or condition of suppurating. "The suppuration of the wound was a clear sign of bacterial infection."

Suppurative (adjective) — used to describe something that involves, causes, or is characterized by suppuration. In medicine, you will see phrases like suppurative otitis media (a middle ear infection that produces pus) or suppurative arthritis (a pus-forming joint infection).

Suppurant (adjective/noun) — something that promotes or causes suppuration; rarely used outside of older medical texts.

If you need to lock this word in your memory permanently, here it is:

To suppurate = for infected tissue to form pus and discharge it. It is the body's infection-driven process of producing and releasing pus from a wound, sore, abscess, or diseased tissue.

Whenever you see "suppurate" or its forms, picture a wound or a boil that is actively infected, swollen, and weeping with pus — that image is exactly what the word means.
